text: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease caused by the breakdown of joint cartilage and underlying bone, and it is considered the most common form of arthritis, affecting approximately 237 million people or 3.3% of the global population as of 2015. It is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide, with an estimated 240 million people experiencing activity-limiting symptoms. The primary symptoms are joint pain and stiffness, which typically progress slowly over years and are worsened by prolonged activity and relieved by rest; morning stiffness usually lasts less than thirty minutes but may return after periods of inactivity. Other symptoms include joint swelling, decreased range of motion, and, when involving the back, weakness or numbness in the arms and legs. The most commonly affected joints are the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers, the base of the thumbs, the knees, hips, neck, and lower back. In smaller joints, Heberden's nodes (on the distal interphalangeal joints) and Bouchard's nodes (on the proximal interphalangeal joints) may form, limiting finger movement, and osteoarthritis of the toes can contribute to bunion development. The condition affects the joints without involving internal organs. Possible causes include prior joint injury, abnormal joint or limb development, inherited factors, mechanical stress on joints, and low-grade inflammatory processes. Risk factors include being overweight, having legs of different lengths, jobs involving high joint stress (such as manual handling, kneeling, squatting, or standing), and a history of joint injury or family history of the disease. Obesity increases the risk of hip and knee osteoarthritis, with those who are obese having twice the risk of developing it. Women, especially post-menopausal women, are more likely to develop osteoarthritis and tend to have more severe symptoms and imaging findings than men, though differences between African Americans and Caucasians remain conflicting. Osteoarthritis is more common in people over 60, with about 10% of males and 18% of females affected. It accounts for about 2% of years lived with disability, and individuals with hip or knee osteoarthritis have a 20% increased risk of mortality, possibly due to reduced activity. Early changes involve a disorganized collagen matrix and reduced proteoglycan content, leading to increased water content in cartilage, while ligaments become thickened, menisci are damaged, and new bone outgrowths (osteophytes) form. Subchondral bone becomes more dense and less mineralized, and inflammation in the joint lining involves macrophages rather than T-cells. Diagnosis is based on clinical signs and symptoms, with X-rays showing joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes, and the combination of joint pain and osteophytes on imaging has good sensitivity and specificity. In 1990, the American College of Rheumatology established criteria for hand osteoarthritis with 92% sensitivity and 98% specificity. Treatment primarily includes lifestyle modifications such as weight loss and exercise, along with pain medications like paracetamol (acetaminophen) and NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen, ibuprofen), which are first-line options. Topical NSAIDs (e.g., diclofenac) may provide relief, though recessed joints respond less well. COX-2 inhibitors are equally effective as nonselective NSAIDs but carry higher cardiovascular risks and are more expensive; rofecoxib was withdrawn in 2004 due to cardiovascular events. Acetaminophen has only a small short-term benefit and may affect liver function, while NSAIDs are more effective for severe pain but carry greater gastrointestinal risks. Opioids are not recommended due to limited benefit and significant risks of addiction and side effects, and their use is reserved for cases where first-line treatments fail. Oral steroids and doxycycline are not recommended. Intra-articular injections of steroids, hyaluronic acid, or platelet-rich plasma may offer short-term pain relief in knee osteoarthritis. Joint injections may be more effective and safer due to increased bioavailability and reduced systemic exposure. Therapeutic exercise, such as walking or swimming, is recommended at least three times per week, under supervision, to reduce pain and improve function, with supervised programs showing the best results for knee osteoarthritis. High-impact exercise increases joint injury risk, while low-impact activities are safer. Functional, gait, and balance training are recommended for lower extremity arthritis to reduce fall risk. For hand osteoarthritis, exercises may offer small benefits in hand function and stiffness. Weak knee extensor muscles may increase the risk of knee osteoarthritis, and strengthening them could prevent it. Lateral wedge insoles and neutral insoles are not helpful, and knee braces have disputed benefits. Heat can relieve stiffness, cold can reduce muscle spasms, and ice massage may improve range of motion, though evidence for pain relief is limited. Hot packs do not reduce swelling, and there is no strong evidence for benefit from hot packs. Education improves self-management and can lead to about 20% more pain relief than NSAIDs alone. If pain relief is not achieved after two weeks, treatment should be reassessed. Remote peer mentorship may help improve self-management in people with socioeconomic disadvantage. Weight loss and exercise are the most safe and effective long-term treatments, with benefits lasting up to six months after a program ends. There is insufficient evidence for massage therapy or manual therapy, and aquatic therapy is safe and effective as an adjunct for knee osteoarthritis, reducing pain and disability in the short term. Medications that alter the disease course have not been found as of 2025. More than 90% of hip and knee joint replacements are due to osteoarthritis, and artificial joints typically last over 20 years.

Several NSAIDs are available for topical use, including diclofenac, which may provide symptomatic relief for osteoarthritis; however, recessed joints, such as the hips, may respond less well to topical therapies. Transdermal opioid pain medications are not typically recommended for osteoarthritis treatment. Topical capsaicin use for osteoarthritis is controversial, as some reviews report benefit while others find no benefit. Intra-articular injections of steroids, hyaluronic acid, or platelet-rich plasma (PRP) may be used for pain relief in knee osteoarthritis. Local drug delivery via intra-articular injection may offer greater effectiveness and safety due to increased bioavailability, less systemic exposure, and reduced adverse events. Several such medications are available. Glucocorticoid injections, such as hydrocortisone, provide short-term pain relief lasting a few weeks to a few months. A 2015 Cochrane review found that knee corticosteroid injections did not improve quality of life or knee joint space, and clinical effects one to six weeks after injection could not be clearly determined due to poor study quality. Higher-dose injections were associated with negative effects in one 2015 study, and a 2017 trial showed reduced cartilage thickness with triamcinolone injections every 12 weeks for two years compared to placebo. A 2018 study linked intra-articular triamcinolone to increased intraocular pressure. High-quality studies on hyaluronic acid injections for hip and knee osteoarthritis only show minor benefit; in other studies, hyaluronic acid injections did not improve knee arthritis compared to placebo and were associated with an increased risk of further pain. Evidence for hyaluronic acid in ankle osteoarthritis is unclear. PRP injections have unclear effectiveness; some suggest they improve function but not pain and are associated with increased risk. A 2014 Cochrane review found the evidence for PRP to be insufficient. Low-dose radiotherapy improves pain and mobility in affected joints, particularly in extremities, with approximately 70–90% effectiveness and minimal side effects. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of sensory knee nerves—also known as genicular neurotomy or genicular RFA—is an outpatient procedure used to reduce knee osteoarthritis pain. During the procedure, a guide cannula is directed under local anesthesia and imaging (ultrasound or fluoroscopy) to each target genicular nerve, and a radiofrequency electrode is passed through it, heating the tip to about 80 °C (176 °F) for one minute to cauterize a segment of the nerve, thereby blocking pain signals. As of 2023, reviews indicate that ablating three or more genicular nerve branches reduces knee pain, with some sources suggesting 4–5 targets may be justified and a 2022 analysis indicating up to 10 targets could provide better long-term pain relief. Pain relief of 50% or more following genicular RFA may last from several months to two years and can be repeated through the same outpatient procedure when pain returns. Phenol injection may be used as a neurolytic treatment to relieve chronic knee osteoarthritis pain. Arthrodesis (joint fusion) may be considered in severe cases of ankle osteoarthritis unresponsive to other treatments. If osteoarthritis symptoms significantly impact quality of life and conservative management fails, joint replacement surgery is an option; evidence supports its use for both knees and hips as clinically effective and cost-effective. People who underwent total knee replacement reported improved quality of life and better pain and function compared to those who did not have surgery, with a less than 1% risk of death within 90 days and less than 5% risk of serious complications (such as prosthetic joint infections, blood clots, or dislocations) after hip or knee replacement. Ninety percent of hip replacement patients and 80% of knee replacement patients reported little or no arthritis-related pain after surgery. Less than 10% of artificial knees and less than 20% of artificial hips required revision over 20 years. Arthroscopic debridement of the knee, also known as joint resurfacing, is not recommended for knee osteoarthritis and has a limited role only in patients with a meniscal tear who have failed other treatments. For shoulder osteoarthritis unresponsive to medications, surgical options include shoulder hemiarthroplasty or total shoulder arthroplasty; demand for these procedures is expected to increase by 750% by 2030. However, there is a lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials to determine which surgical approach is most effective, the associated risks, or how it compares to other treatments. Low-quality evidence suggests no significant short-term clinical benefit when comparing total shoulder arthroplasty to hemiarthroplasty, and it is unclear whether the risk of harm differs between the two. Osteotomy may be useful in knee osteoarthritis but has not been well studied and its effectiveness relative to non-surgical treatments or other surgeries is unclear. Arthroscopic surgery is not recommended for knee osteoarthritis as it does not improve outcomes and may cause harm; its benefit in mild to moderate cases is unclear. Glucosamine’s effectiveness is controversial; reviews show it is equal to or slightly better than placebo, with possible differences between glucosamine sulfate (which shows benefit) and glucosamine hydrochloride (which does not). Evidence for glucosamine sulfate affecting disease progression is unclear and likely modest. The Osteoarthritis Research Society International recommends discontinuing glucosamine if no effect is seen after six months, and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence no longer recommends its use. Despite uncertainty, glucosamine remains a treatment option. The European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis recommends glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfate for knee osteoarthritis. Its use is generally safe. A 2015 Cochrane review of chondroitin found most trials were of low quality, but some evidence of short-term pain improvement with few side effects; it does not appear to improve or maintain joint health. Avocado–soybean unsaponifiables (ASU), an extract from avocado and soybean oils sold as a dietary supplement or prescription drug in France, may provide short-term pain relief in some osteoarthritis patients, but does not improve or maintain joint health. A two-year high-quality trial comparing ASU to chondroitin found no difference between them, and there is insufficient evidence on ASU safety. Only a few moderate-quality studies of Boswellia serrata show small improvements in pain and function. Curcumin and s-adenosyl methionine (SAMe) show little effect on pain; a 2009 Cochrane review recommended against routine SAMe use due to insufficient high-quality research. A 2021 review found hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) had no benefit in reducing pain or improving physical function in hand or knee osteoarthritis, and its off-label use should be discouraged. There is no evidence for colchicine in treating hand or knee arthritis pain. Limited evidence supports the use of hyaluronan, methylsulfonylmethane, rose hip, capsaicin, or vitamin D. Acupuncture provides small pain relief, which may be of questionable importance, and waiting list–controlled trials show clinically relevant benefits possibly due to placebo effects; long-term benefits are not established. TENS and low-level laser therapy have no conclusive evidence of reducing pain or disability; one review found unclear benefit, while another found short-term pain relief for osteoarthritic knees. Research is needed to determine if balneotherapy improves quality of life or function. Low-quality evidence suggests therapeutic ultrasound may be beneficial for knee osteoarthritis, though further research is needed; it is safe, reduces pain, and improves physical function, while phonophoresis may offer greater pain relief than standard non-drug ultrasound. Weak evidence suggests electromagnetic field treatment may provide moderate pain relief, but further research is needed to determine if it improves quality of life or function. Globally, as of 2010, approximately 250 million people had knee osteoarthritis (3.6% of the population), and hip osteoarthritis affected about 0.85% of the population. In 2004, osteoarthritis caused moderate to severe disability in 43.4 million people, ranking as the 11th most disabling condition globally among 291 diseases. In the Middle East and North Africa, hip osteoarthritis prevalence increased three-fold (from 1.28 million to 1.28 million cases) from 1990 to 2019, and knee osteoarthritis increased 2.88-fold (from 6.16 million to 17.75 million cases). Hand osteoarthritis in MENA increased 2.7-fold (from 1.6 million to 4.3 million cases). As of 2012, osteoarthritis affected 52.5 million people in the United States, about 50% of whom were 65 years or older; 80% of the population have radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis by age 65, though only 60% experience symptoms. The U.S. rate is projected to reach 78 million (26%) adults by 2040. In 2011, there were approximately 964,000 hospitalizations for osteoarthritis, at a rate of 31 stays per 10,000 population, with an aggregate cost of $14.8 billion ($15,400 per stay), making it the second-most expensive condition in U.S. hospital stays and the second-most costly billed to Medicare and private insurance. In Europe, osteoarthritis prevalence increased from 27.9 million in 1990 to 50.8 million in 2019; hand osteoarthritis was the second most prevalent type, affecting 12.5 million people. In 2019, knee osteoarthritis was the 18th most common cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) in Europe, accounting for 1.28% of all YLDs (up from 1.12% in 1990). In India, osteoarthritis increased from 23.46 million in 1990 to 62.35 million in 2019; knee osteoarthritis was the most prevalent type, followed by hand osteoarthritis. In 2019, osteoarthritis was the 20th most common cause of YLDs in India (1.48% of all YLDs), up from 1.25% and previously the 23rd most common cause. Osteoarthritis comes from the Greek "ostéon" (bone) and "arthritis" (joint inflammation), though inflammation is not a prominent feature; some clinicians use "osteoarthrosis" to emphasize the non-inflammatory nature. The condition has been reported in various animals, including cats, rodents, cattle, deer, rabbits, sheep, camels, elephants, buffalo, hyenas, lions, mules, pigs, tigers, kangaroos, dolphins, dugongs, and horses, and in fossils of the dinosaur Allosaurus fragilis. Disease-modifying therapies aim to alter disease progression by arresting structural joint changes and ameliorating symptoms. Emerging evidence suggests a system-based approach is needed to identify osteoarthritis causes. A University of Twente study found that osmolarity-induced intracellular molecular crowding may drive disease pathology. Guidelines for including soluble biomarkers in osteoarthritis clinical trials were published in 2015, but as of 2021, no validated biomarkers are used clinically. Osteoarthritis has been observed in the fossils of the large carnivorous dinosaur Allosaurus fragilis. Pharmaceutical agents that modify the natural course of the disease by halting joint structural deterioration and relieving symptoms are referred to as disease-modifying therapies. Current therapies under investigation include various agents aimed at altering disease progression. There is growing evidence that a system-based approach is required to identify the underlying causes of osteoarthritis; a study by scientists at the University of Twente suggested that osmolarity-induced intracellular molecular crowding may contribute to disease pathology. Guidelines for including soluble biomarkers in osteoarthritis clinical trials were published in 2015, but as of 2021, no validated biomarkers are used clinically to diagnose osteoarthritis. A 2015 systematic review of biomarkers for osteoarthritis, analyzing 25 publications, identified 37 different biochemical markers of bone and cartilage turnover. The strongest evidence supported urinary C-terminal telopeptide of type II collagen (uCTX-II) as a prognostic marker for knee osteoarthritis progression and serum cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) levels as a prognostic marker for both knee and hip osteoarthritis incidence. A review of biomarkers in hip osteoarthritis also noted associations with uCTX-II. Procollagen type II C-terminal propeptide (PIICP) levels indicate type II collagen synthesis in the body and within joint fluid, and PIICP levels can serve as a prognostic marker for early osteoarthritis.
